kurals.tamil:
வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகைமற் றெல்லாம்
குறியெதிர்ப்பை நீர துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Variyaarkku ondru eevadhe eekai matru ellaam
Kuriyedhirppai neeradhu udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Only what is given to those who have nothing is true giving; every other gift carries the character of a calculated exchange that expects something back.
kurals.elementary: If you give your friend a sticker because you hope they will give you one back, that is really a trade. But if you give your lunch to a kid who has no lunch at all and can never pay you back, that is real giving. This kural says only the second kind counts as true giving.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition by exclusion: ஈகை (eekai) is giving to the வறியார் (the destitute), and everything else is குறியெதிர்ப்பை — a gift made with a ‘measured return’ in view, which the old commentators read as something close to a loan or a reciprocal obligation. The move sharply separates philanthropy from the neighbouring virtue of ஒப்புரவு (social beneficence, Chapter 22) and from ordinary gift exchange, which anthropologists since Marcel Mauss have shown to be governed by expectations of return. The criterion is not the size of the gift but the incapacity of the recipient to repay; that incapacity is what guarantees the purity of the motive. The same test appears in Jesus’ advice to invite those who ‘cannot recompense thee’ and in the Gita’s definition of sattvic gifts given ‘without expectation of return’, making this one of the most widely shared ethical intuitions across traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That gift which is given out of duty, at the proper time and place, to a worthy person, and without expectation of return, is considered to be charity in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks gifts by motive; the highest (sattvic) gift is given simply because it ought to be given, with no return expected from the recipient.
hinduism.tie_back: Same core test as the Kural: a gift that expects a return is not the highest kind of giving. The Gita adds conditions of time, place and a ‘worthy’ recipient, whereas Valluvar makes need itself the qualification.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on ‘no expectation of return’; differs in that the Gita emphasises a worthy recipient rather than a destitute one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee. But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his host that feeding people who can invite you back is just an exchange; feeding the poor, who cannot repay, is what is truly blessed.
christianity.tie_back: Almost a paraphrase of the Kural: giving to those who can return the favour is reciprocity, giving to the needy is real generosity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: both define true giving by the recipient’s inability to repay.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive, [Saying], ‘We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.’”
islam.explanation: The righteous feed the poor, orphans and captives while explicitly refusing any reward or even thanks from them.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s two elements: the recipient is the needy, and nothing is expected back from them.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close; the Qur’an grounds the gift in seeking God’s approval, a religious motive the Kural leaves unstated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A lower level than this is one who gives charity to the poor without knowing to whom he gave and without the poor person knowing from whom he received. For this is an observance of the mitzvah for its sake alone.”
judaism.explanation: In his ladder of eight levels of charity, Maimonides ranks anonymous giving very high because no relationship, gratitude or debt can form between giver and receiver.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Maimonides values the gift that cannot turn into an exchange; anonymity removes any chance of repayment.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:8 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong shared principle (giving free of any return), reached through anonymity; Maimonides places enabling self-sufficiency even higher (10:7).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He gives a gift with the thought, ‘I am well-off. These are not well-off. It would not be right for me, being well-off, not to give a gift to those who are not well-off.’”
buddhism.explanation: In the Dana Sutta the Buddha ranks motives for giving; giving because others are in need ranks above giving to store up rewards for oneself after death.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s focus on need as the reason to give and its low view of gifts made for personal profit.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.49, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic parallel; the sutta ranks this motive in the middle of a hierarchy rather than defining it as the only true gift.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farmer’s wisdom treats giving as a system of reciprocity: you give to those who will give back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An instructive contrast. Hesiod describes exactly the ‘measured return’ kind of giving that Valluvar says does not count as ஈகை at all.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 353-355 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel: archaic Greek ethics of reciprocity is the position the Kural rejects.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Therefore the liberal man, like other virtuous men, will give for the sake of the noble, and rightly; for he will give to the right people, the right amounts, and at the right time.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the generous person gives because giving well is noble, not to gain something, and gives to the right recipients.
philosophy.tie_back: Agrees with the Kural that true giving is not motivated by return; Aristotle leaves ‘the right people’ open, while Valluvar specifies the destitute.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shared rejection of self-interested giving; Aristotle’s criterion of the ‘right people’ is broader than Valluvar’s focus on the needy.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல்தீது மேலுலகம்
இல்லெனினும் ஈதலே நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallaaru eninum kolal theedhu melulagam
Illeninum eedhale nandru.
kurals.meaning: Even if someone calls taking from others a good path, taking is still bad; and even if there were no heaven to gain by it, giving would still be good.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone says, “It’s fine to always ask for other people’s snacks.” It still isn’t a good habit. And imagine someone says, “Sharing won’t win you any prize.” Sharing is still the right thing to do. Giving is good even if nobody rewards you for it.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on two concessive clauses (எனினும், ‘even if’) that strip away the usual religious sanctions: receiving is wrong even if called a நல்லாறு (good path), and giving is right even if there is no மேலுலகம் (heaven above). Parimelazhagar reads the first line as rejecting the idea that accepting alms could be meritorious, which touches a live debate in Indian thought where receiving gifts was a recognised livelihood for some groups. The second line is philosophically bolder: it makes the value of giving independent of any afterlife reward, anticipating the distinction between acting from duty and acting from hope of reward. Valluvar thus grounds generosity in its intrinsic goodness rather than in cosmic bookkeeping.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that right action should be done for its own sake, without attachment to what it will bring you.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to giving: give because it is good, not because it earns heaven.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General principle of acting without desire for results, not specific to charity; matches the Kural’s second line well, not its first.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes Jesus to say that giving is a greater good than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s ranking: receiving is lesser, giving is better.
christianity._accuracy_note: Captures the give/receive contrast; lacks the Kural’s explicit claim that giving is good even without heavenly reward.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is that of the giver and the lower (hand) is that of the beggar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, speaking about charity and about refraining from begging, said the hand that gives is better than the hand that asks.
islam.tie_back: Same judgement as the Kural’s first line: asking and taking are lower; giving is better.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the give/take hierarchy; the hadith does not address the ‘even without heaven’ clause.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should always construct [sic] himself and bear hardship rather than appeal to people at large and make himself a burden on the community.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides urges people to endure hardship rather than depend on others’ charity if they can possibly avoid it.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s first line that taking from others is to be avoided even when it seems acceptable.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:18 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the anti-dependence line; Maimonides also insists (10:19) that the truly needy must accept help, a nuance absent from the Kural. Quoted verbatim; the source’s ‘construct’ is evidently a typo for ‘constrict’ (Hebrew yidchok, ‘press/constrain’).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person gives a gift seeking his own profit, with a mind attached [to the reward], seeking to store up for himself [with the thought], ‘I’ll enjoy this after death.’”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes this as the lowest motive for giving; higher gifts are given without calculating an afterlife reward.
buddhism.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s second line: giving aimed at securing heaven is inferior to giving done because it is good.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.49, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on devaluing reward-seeking gifts, though the sutta still assigns heavenly results to every level of giving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give is a good girl, but Take is bad and she brings death.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod personifies Giving and Taking as two women: one good, the other deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: taking is bad, giving is good.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 356 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Direct verbal parallel on give vs. take, though Hesiod’s ‘Take’ refers chiefly to grasping or seizing rather than accepting alms.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be tardy in coming forward to be the objects of their kindness; for it is not noble to be keen to receive benefits.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says a good person should be slow to accept favours, since eagerness to receive is not noble.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s claim that receiving is ignoble even when socially accepted.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the first half; Aristotle speaks of friends’ favours rather than alms, and says nothing of heaven.

kurals.tamil:
இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை ஈதல்
குலனுடையான் கண்ணே யுள.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilan ennum evvam uraiyaamai eedhal
Kulanudaiyaan kanne ula.
kurals.meaning: Not uttering the miserable words “I have nothing,” and giving anyway, are found only in a person of true nobility.
kurals.elementary: When someone asks for help, it is easy to say, “Sorry, I don’t have anything.” A truly good person doesn’t hide behind that excuse. Even when they have only a little, they find something to share.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the phrase இலன் என்னும் எவ்வம், ‘the misery of saying “I have not”’. Commentators divide on whose words these are: Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read it as giving before the needy person has to humiliate himself by declaring his poverty, while others (e.g. Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as the giver not pleading poverty himself even when he is in straitened circumstances. Both readings put the burden of dignity on the giver: generosity is shown most clearly when one’s means are small or the asker’s shame can be spared. குலன் (kulan), usually glossed ‘noble birth’, is best understood as nobility of character and upbringing, in line with the Kural’s repeated view that conduct, not birth, defines a person (cf. Kural 972).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s Ashvamedhika Parva, a starving Brahmin family who live by gleaning grain give their only meal of barley flour to a hungry guest, one after another, rather than turn him away. A mongoose that rolls in the spilled flour finds half its body turned to gold, and later declares that Yudhishthira’s grand horse-sacrifice was not equal to this poor family’s gift.
hinduism.explanation: The story teaches that a small gift given from poverty outweighs lavish gifts given from abundance.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ideal: a household with almost nothing does not plead poverty, but gives.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva (Anugita section), story of the mongoose and the Brahmin’s flour
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode; the story is a close narrative illustration of giving from scarcity without saying ‘I have nothing’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises a poor widow whose two small coins, given out of her poverty, were worth more than the large gifts of the rich.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours the person who gives despite having little, instead of pleading poverty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match with the reading of the Kural as ‘giving without pleading one’s own poverty’.

islam.quote_or_event: “They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what they [i.e., the emigrants] were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the Ansar of Medina, who shared with the refugees from Mecca and put them first even while poor themselves.
islam.tie_back: Same ideal of giving from one’s own want rather than pleading it.
islam._accuracy_note: Close parallel: preference for others ‘even though they are in privation’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands that one must not close one’s hand to a poor person but give generously for his need.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s refusal to turn away the asker; the ‘shut hand’ corresponds to the evasive ‘I have nothing’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the command not to refuse; does not address giving from one’s own poverty or noble character specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak the truth; yield not to anger; when asked, give even if you only have a little. By these three means can one reach the presence of the gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada tells people to give when asked even if they have only a little.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural: when someone asks, don’t say ‘I have nothing’; give from the little you have.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match with the giver-centred reading of the Kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 14, the swineherd Eumaeus, a poor servant, welcomes the disguised Odysseus as a ragged stranger, kills two of his own pigs to feed him, and tells him that strangers and beggars come from Zeus and that even a small gift is welcome.
greek_mythology.explanation: A man of humble means makes no excuse of poverty and shares what he has with a beggar.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eumaeus shows the Kural’s nobility of character: giving generously from little, without pleading want.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode; strong narrative parallel, framed by the Greek ethic of hospitality (xenia) rather than charity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I can find nothing to give you which is worthy of you; I feel my poverty in this respect alone. Therefore I present you with the only thing I possess, myself.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells how Aeschines, a poor pupil of Socrates, gave himself when he had no money, and how Socrates valued this above the rich pupils’ gifts.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it praises the person who does not use poverty as an excuse but finds something to give.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits I.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good parallel on giving from poverty; the context is a gift to a teacher rather than alms to the needy.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல் இரந்தவர்
இன்முகங் காணும் அளவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaadhu irakkap padudhal irandhavar
Inmugam kaanum alavu.
kurals.meaning: Being asked for help is painful to a generous person, but only until they see the asker’s face light up with joy.
kurals.elementary: When a friend is sad and asks for help, you feel a little sad too. But when you help them and they smile, your sadness melts away. This kural says the giver’s pain lasts only until they see that smile.
kurals.university: The verb இரக்கப்படுதல், ‘to be begged of’, frames the scene from the giver’s side: Parimelazhagar explains that the sight of a suppliant’s distress is itself painful to a compassionate person. That pain ends at a precise moment — அளவு, ‘up to the point’ — when the giver sees the இன்முகம், the pleasant face, of the one who has been helped. The couplet therefore locates the reward of giving in shared emotion rather than in merit, reputation or return. It also implies a standard for how to give: the gift must be large and gracious enough to change the receiver’s face, which links it with teachings such as Maimonides’ rule that charity must be given with a pleasant countenance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But charity performed with the expectation of some return, or with a desire for fruitive results, or in a grudging mood, is said to be charity in the mode of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes grudging, reluctant giving as a lower (rajasic) kind of charity.
hinduism.tie_back: By implication the right way to give is gladly; the Kural pictures the giver’s joy when the receiver brightens.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Indirect match: the Gita condemns grudging gifts but does not describe the giver sharing the recipient’s joy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks Christians to give willingly and cheerfully rather than reluctantly.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s emotional picture of giving: sorrow gives way to gladness in the act of giving.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the joyful spirit; the Kural’s specific detail (seeing the receiver’s happy face) is not present.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders [of it] or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says charity is cancelled if the giver hurts the receiver by reminding them of it or humiliating them.
islam.tie_back: Both texts care about the receiver’s feelings; a gift is complete only when it leaves the receiver glad, not wounded.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel concern for the recipient’s dignity; framed as a prohibition rather than as the giver’s joy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whenever a person gives charity to a poor person with an unpleasant countenance and with his face buried in the earth, he loses and destroys his merit even if he gives him 1000 gold pieces.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that charity given with a sour face loses its merit; it must be given with a pleasant face and with joy, sympathising with the poor person.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the receiver’s இன்முகம் (pleasant face); Maimonides insists on the giver’s. Both make faces and feelings central to true giving.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:4 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong emotional and ‘countenance’ parallel, seen from the giver’s side rather than the receiver’s.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Before giving, glad; while giving, the mind is bright & clear; having given, one is gratified: This is the consummation of the sacrifice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the ideal donor’s state of mind as joyful before, during and after the gift.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts joy at the end of a true act of giving.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37, Dana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the giver’s gladness; the Kural roots that gladness in seeing the receiver’s joy, which the sutta does not mention.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey Book 17, the suitor Antinous refuses the disguised Odysseus, who is begging for food, insults him, and throws a footstool at him, while others at the feast give him scraps. Even the other suitors warn that the gods sometimes walk among men disguised as strangers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous is the anti-model of a giver: he meets a beggar’s plea with contempt and violence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A contrast to the Kural: instead of sharing the suppliant’s pain and ending it by giving, Antinous adds to it — and later dies first when Odysseus takes revenge.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a negative example that illustrates the Kural by contrast rather than by agreement.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Above all we should give willingly, quickly, and without any hesitation; a benefit commands no gratitude if it has hung for a long time in the hands of the giver, if he seems unwilling to part with it, and gives it as though he were being robbed of it.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that the manner of giving matters: a gift given reluctantly loses its value.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s picture of a giver who hurries to end the asker’s pain and delights in the result.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits II.1 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good parallel on prompt, willing giving; Seneca’s focus is on gratitude and the benefit relation rather than on shared joy.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பசிஆற்றல் அப்பசியை
மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral pasi aatral appasiyai
Maatruvaar aatralin pin.
kurals.meaning: The strength of ascetics lies in enduring hunger, but that strength ranks below the strength of those who relieve the hunger of others.
kurals.elementary: Going without food on purpose takes a lot of strength. But this kural says there is an even greater strength: giving food to someone who is hungry. Helping others beats showing how tough you are.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the word ஆற்றல் (power, strength) and the verb ஆற்று (to endure, to perform): the ascetics’ power is பசி ஆற்றல், the power to endure hunger, whereas the philanthropist’s power is to மாற்று (change, remove) hunger. Valluvar deliberately ranks the householder’s charity above the ascetic’s self-mortification — a notable claim in a culture that deeply honoured tapas, and consistent with the Kural’s high regard for the householder (Chapter 5). The same contrast between self-denial and feeding the hungry is made by Isaiah, who says the fast God wants is to ‘deal thy bread to the hungry’. The couplet effectively redefines spiritual strength in social terms.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from suffering.”
hinduism.explanation: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away his food and water to hungry visitors and declares that he wants neither yogic powers nor liberation, only to relieve others’ suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: Rantideva puts relieving others’ hunger above mystic attainments won by austerity — the same ranking as the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel: an ascetic king values feeding the hungry above yogic perfection.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink... Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Last Judgement, Jesus identifies himself with the hungry and says feeding them is serving him.
christianity.tie_back: Feeding the hungry is treated as the highest religious act, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Affirms the supreme value of feeding the hungry; does not explicitly compare it with fasting.

islam.quote_or_event: “But he has not broken through the difficult pass. And what can make you know what is [breaking through] the difficult pass? It is the freeing of a slave Or feeding on a day of severe hunger An orphan of near relationship Or a needy person in misery.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls feeding the hungry in a time of famine ‘the difficult pass’, a steep and demanding climb.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it frames relieving hunger as the true test of strength.
islam._accuracy_note: Close: feeding the hungry as the hard, high path; no explicit comparison with ascetic fasting.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah tells people who fast that God prefers them to share their bread with the hungry.
judaism.tie_back: Near-identical ranking to the Kural: feeding the hungry is valued above going hungry oneself.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both explicitly place relieving hunger above fasting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta is born as a hare who, having no food to offer a hungry brahmin visitor (the god Sakka in disguise), leaps into a fire so that his own body may be eaten. Sakka honours the gift by painting the hare’s image on the moon.
buddhism.explanation: The hare offers the ultimate gift, its own body, to relieve a stranger’s hunger.
buddhism.tie_back: Relieving hunger is shown as the highest act of virtue, beyond any feat of self-control.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong on feeding the hungry as supreme virtue, but lacks the Kural’s explicit comparison with ascetic endurance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to mortals so that they can cook food and survive, and is punished by Zeus by being chained to a rock where an eagle eats his liver.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus uses his power not for himself but to meet human need, at great cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours power used to relieve others’ want above power used for oneself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a loose thematic parallel about using power for others’ survival, not specifically about hunger versus fasting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it.”
philosophy.explanation: Peter Singer argues that people who can relieve starvation at modest cost are morally obliged to do so.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Singer makes the relief of hunger a central moral demand and a measure of moral strength.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shared priority on relieving hunger; Singer argues from utilitarian obligation, not from a comparison with asceticism.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல் அஃதொருவன்
பெற்றான் பொருள்வைப் புழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Atraar azhipasi theerththal agdhoruvan
Petraan porul vaippuzhi.
kurals.meaning: Relieving the killing hunger of the destitute is the place where a person who has gained wealth should store it.
kurals.elementary: People keep money in a piggy bank or a bank to keep it safe. This kural says the safest place to keep your money is in a hungry person’s full stomach. When you feed someone, your wealth becomes goodness that can never be stolen.
kurals.university: The couplet takes the image of a treasury (பொருள் வைப்புழி, ‘the place where wealth is deposited’) and relocates it: the proper strongroom for wealth is the relief of அழிபசி, ‘destroying hunger’, suffered by those who have nothing (அற்றார்). The metaphor inverts ordinary prudence, which stores wealth by withholding it, and claims that wealth is truly secured only by giving it away. Commentators read this both as moral merit that follows the giver into future lives and as social security in this life. The same ‘treasury’ inversion appears in Jesus’ ‘treasures in heaven’, in King Munbaz’s reply in the Talmud and in the Buddhist ‘well-stored fund’ of Khp 8, showing a widely shared intuition that generosity is the only wealth immune to loss.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the rich satisfy the poor implorer, and bend his eye upon a longer pathway. Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn on Liberality urges the rich to feed the poor and look to the long run, since wealth never stays in one place.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats feeding the poor as the far-sighted use of wealth that cannot be kept anyway.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic parallel on the wise use of fleeting wealth; lacks the explicit ‘storehouse’ image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly treasure with lasting heavenly treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Same ‘true storehouse’ inversion as the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in metaphor; the Kural names feeding the hungry as the specific deposit, Matthew is more general here.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains. And Allāh multiplies [His reward] for whom He wills.”
islam.explanation: Wealth spent in God’s way is compared to a seed that multiplies many times over.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, giving is presented not as loss but as the best investment of wealth.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel idea (giving preserves and multiplies wealth) using a seed image rather than a storehouse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My ancestors stored up below, whereas I am storing above... My ancestors stored up treasures in a place where the human hand can reach, and so their treasures could have been robbed, whereas I am storing up treasures in a place where the human hand cannot reach.”
judaism.explanation: King Munbaz, criticised for spending his family treasure on the poor during a drought, replies that he is storing it in a safer place.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: relieving hunger in famine is the true treasury of wealth.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 11a (William Davidson/Koren translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both use the storehouse metaphor for feeding the hungry.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But when a man or woman has laid aside a well-stored fund of generosity, virtue, restraint, & self-control... That’s a well-stored fund. It can’t be wrested away. It follows you along.”
buddhism.explanation: The Reserve Fund discourse compares buried treasure, which can be lost, with the ‘fund’ of generosity, which cannot.
buddhism.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural: generosity is where wealth is kept safe.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel; the Buddhist text lists generosity among several virtues rather than feeding the hungry specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s tale, the poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon share their meagre meal with two disguised gods whom everyone else in the village had turned away. The gods flood the village but turn the couple’s cottage into a temple and grant their wish to serve there together and to die at the same moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple’s generosity from poverty becomes their lasting reward.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their small gift of food turns out to be the safest ‘deposit’ they ever made, as the Kural suggests.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; narrative illustration of generosity rewarded, within the framework of divine hospitality rather than charity to the poor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These fine things show their quality better in the spending than in the hoarding... money is only precious when it is given away.”
philosophy.explanation: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that riches have value only when they are spent or given, not when they are piled up.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates the value of wealth from keeping it to giving it.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy II, Prose 5 (tr. W. V. Cooper)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on giving as the true value of wealth; Boethius’ aim is to show wealth is not a true good, not to promote charity.

kurals.tamil:
பாத்தூண் மரீஇ யவனைப் பசியென்னும்
தீப்பிணி தீண்டல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Paaththoon mareeiyavanaip pasiyennum
Theeppini theendal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: The fiery disease called hunger will hardly ever touch someone who has made it a habit to share their food with others.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who always shares their snacks at school. When that kid forgets their lunch one day, everyone is happy to share with them. People who share food are rarely left hungry.
kurals.university: பாத்தூண் (pāththūṇ) means ‘divided food’, food portioned out and shared, and மரீஇ indicates something practised until it is second nature. Hunger is called தீப்பிணி, a ‘fiery disease’ or ‘evil illness’, strengthening the medical image in which sharing works as a kind of immunity. The claim can be read at three levels: morally, as merit protecting the giver; socially, as a web of reciprocity in which those who share are shared with; and economically, as the observation that shared resources are used more efficiently. The Dhammapada’s ‘Hunger is the worst disease’ and the hadith that ‘food for two is sufficient for three’ show how widespread both the disease image and the sufficiency claim are.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “THE Gods have not ordained hunger to be our death: even to the well-fed man comes death in varied shape. The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn to Liberality says the generous never run out, while the stingy are left without help.
hinduism.tie_back: Same promise as the Kural: those who share will not be abandoned to want.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close parallel, including the hunger theme; the hymn stresses the giver’s riches not wasting rather than immunity from hunger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that those who give will receive generously in return.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, generosity is said to protect the giver from want.
christianity._accuracy_note: General promise of return to the giver; not specific to food or hunger.

islam.quote_or_event: “The food for two persons is sufficient for three, and the food of three persons is sufficient for four persons.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that food, when shared, stretches to feed more people.
islam.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s claim that sharing food, far from leaving one hungry, provides enough for all.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on sharing food and sufficiency; does not speak of the sharer’s own protection from hunger.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person will never become impoverished from giving charity. No harm nor damage will ever be caused because of charity.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides states as a principle that giving charity never makes anyone poor.
judaism.tie_back: The same assurance as the Kural: the habitual giver is protected from want.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Matanot Aniyim 10:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close parallel; Maimonides speaks of poverty in general rather than hunger specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hunger is the worst disease, conditioned things the worst suffering. Knowing this as it really is, the wise realize Nibbana, the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls hunger the worst of diseases.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s striking image of hunger as a disease (தீப்பிணி), though it uses it to point to spiritual release rather than sharing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbal parallel on ‘hunger as disease’; the ethical point (sharing prevents hunger) is not in this verse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, King Erysichthon cuts down a sacred oak of Ceres and scorns the gods. Ceres sends Famine (Fames) to breathe insatiable hunger into him; he eats away his whole fortune, sells his daughter, and finally devours his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hunger is portrayed as a personified curse that consumes a greedy, impious man.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The mirror image of the Kural: the man who respects nothing and shares nothing is the one the ‘fiery disease’ of hunger devours.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a contrast myth. Erysichthon’s crime is sacrilege and arrogance rather than failure to share food.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant’s fourth example in the Groundwork imagines a prosperous man who refuses to help others in hardship. Kant argues that he cannot will this as a universal law, because many situations may arise in which he himself would need the love and sympathy of others and would then have robbed himself of all hope of help.
philosophy.explanation: Kant shows that a world without mutual help is one nobody could rationally choose, because everyone may one day be in need.
philosophy.tie_back: Offers a rational basis for the Kural’s claim: those who share are part of a practice of mutual aid that protects them too.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section II (Ak. 4:423)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Kant’s point is logical consistency of the maxim, not a practical promise that givers will not go hungry.

kurals.tamil:
ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம் அறியார்கொல் தாமுடைமை
வைத்திழக்கும் வன்க ணவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Eeththuvakkum inbam ariyaarkol thaamudaimai
Vaiththizhakkum vankanavar.
kurals.meaning: Do the hard-hearted, who hoard their possessions only to lose them in the end, not know the joy of giving and rejoicing in it?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who hides all his toys in a box so nobody else can play with them. The toys get old, break, or get lost, and he never had fun sharing them. This kural asks: doesn’t he know how happy it feels to give?
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question (அறியார்கொல், ‘do they not know?’) directed at the வன்கணவர், literally ‘the hard-eyed’, a Tamil idiom for the pitiless and miserly. Its irony lies in the verb pair வைத்து இழக்கும், ‘keep and lose’: the miser keeps wealth in order not to lose it, yet loses it anyway, through death, theft or decay, having missed the one pleasure it could have given. ஈத்து உவக்கும் இன்பம், ‘the joy of giving and delighting’, is presented as a real and distinct pleasure available only to the giver. The argument is almost psychological rather than moral: miserliness is not only wrong but self-defeating.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by teaching that everything in the world is pervaded by the Lord; one should enjoy it through renunciation and not covet anyone’s wealth, since wealth truly belongs to no one.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad teaches that clinging to possessions misunderstands their nature, since nothing we hold is ultimately ours.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it exposes the futility of hoarding what cannot be kept; joy comes from letting go.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; parallel on the futility of possessiveness, but not specifically about the joy of giving.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Rich Fool, a man hoards his harvest for himself and dies that very night, losing everything.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ‘keep and lose’: the hoarder stores up wealth only to lose it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on hoarding and loss; the joy of giving is implied rather than stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty ever think that it is better for them. Rather, it is worse for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns misers that their hoarded wealth will become a burden around their necks.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says hoarding does not benefit the hoarder, even though he thinks it does.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the self-defeat of miserliness; expressed as eschatological punishment rather than a lost joy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes laments wealth that is hoarded, then lost, leaving nothing behind.
judaism.tie_back: Close parallel to the Kural’s ‘hoard and lose’ (வைத்திழக்கும்).
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on hoarding and losing; lacks the Kural’s positive image of the joy of giving.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada contrasts misers with the wise person who rejoices in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: the miser misses the joy that the giver knows.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close parallel on the joy of giving versus miserliness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the man who gives willingly, even though he gives a great thing, rejoices in his gift and is glad in heart; but whoever gives way to shamelessness and takes something himself, even though it be a small thing, it freezes his heart.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says willing givers feel gladness while grasping takers feel their hearts go cold.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a real joy that belongs only to the giver.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 357-360 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on the giver’s joy; Hesiod contrasts it with taking rather than with hoarding.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”
philosophy.explanation: Andrew Carnegie argued that the wealthy should give away their surplus fortunes during their lifetime rather than hold on to them until death.
philosophy.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s charge that the hoarder only keeps his wealth to lose it at death, missing the chance to give.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the disgrace of dying with hoarded wealth; Carnegie focuses on social duty rather than the personal joy of giving.

kurals.tamil:
இரத்தலின் இன்னாது மன்ற நிரப்பிய
தாமே தமியர் உணல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iraththalin innaadhu mandra nirappiya
Thaame thamiyar unal.
kurals.meaning: Eating alone and unshared, just to keep one’s stores full, is surely more miserable than begging.
kurals.elementary: Begging for food feels bad. But this kural says something feels even worse: sitting alone with a big pile of food and never sharing any of it. Being lonely and greedy is sadder than being poor.
kurals.university: The comparison is deliberately shocking. In Chapter 106 (இரவு) and elsewhere, begging is treated as the lowest and most painful condition, yet here Valluvar says solitary eating is more இன்னாது (painful, wretched) than begging, and seals it with மன்ற, ‘certainly’. நிரப்பிய is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in order to fill up’ one’s wealth, so the target is not eating as such but the miser who refuses to share lest his stores shrink. தமியர் உணல் (eating alone) stands for a whole social failure; the Rig Veda makes the same point when it says the man who eats without a companion is ‘all guilt’, and Epicurus says a meal without a friend is the life of a lion or wolf.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The foolish man wins food with fruitless labour: that food -I speak the truth- shall be his ruin. He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Vedic hymn to Liberality condemns the man who eats alone without sharing, saying he is nothing but sin.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact parallel to the Kural’s condemnation of solitary eating (see also Gita 3.13: those who cook only for themselves ‘eat only sin’).
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on eating alone as the worst condition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus, the rich man feasts alone while a beggar starves at his gate; after death their fates are reversed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the parable judges the solitary feaster’s state to be worse than the beggar’s.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel: the unshared feast is condemned and the beggar ends up better off.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? For that is the one who drives away the orphan And does not encourage the feeding of the poor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an links refusing to feed the poor with denying the Day of Judgement.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats refusal to share food as a serious moral failure.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel condemnation of not feeding the poor; no explicit comparison with begging.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of character in human beings: One that says: ‘mine is mine, and yours is yours’: this is a commonplace type; and some say this is a sodom-type of character.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah says the attitude ‘what’s mine is mine’ is, according to some, the character of Sodom, the city proverbial for refusing hospitality.
judaism.tie_back: The solitary eater of the Kural is exactly this ‘mine is mine’ person, judged harshly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel on condemning refusal to share; not about food or a comparison with begging.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without having shared, if there were someone to receive their gift.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that anyone who understood the fruits of sharing would never eat without first giving.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural’s condemnation of eating alone and unshared.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both single out eating without sharing as the failure of generosity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches become gold. His wish is granted, but his bread and wine turn to gold as he touches them, and he sits alone amid his treasure, starving, until he begs the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas’ greed for gold leaves him hungry and isolated in the middle of great riches.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s point that hoarding for oneself can be more wretched than poverty.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a loose parallel on the misery of greed, not specifically about refusing to share food.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “You must reflect carefully beforehand with whom you are to eat and drink, rather than what you are to eat and drink. For a dinner of meats without the company of a friend is like the life of a lion or a wolf.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca quotes Epicurus, who held that eating without companions reduces a human being to the level of a solitary predator.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats solitary eating as a degradation of human life.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 19.10, quoting Epicurus (tr. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the wretchedness of eating alone; Epicurus’ concern is friendship, not charity to the needy.

kurals.tamil:
சாதலின் இன்னாத தில்லை இனிததூஉம்
ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Saadhalin innaadhadhu illai inidhadhooum
Eedhal iyaiyaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: Nothing is more painful than death; yet even death becomes sweet when one is no longer able to give.
kurals.elementary: Everyone thinks the worst thing in the world is dying. But this kural says a truly kind person would feel even worse if they could never help anyone again. For them, being unable to give is the saddest thing of all.
kurals.university: The final couplet of the chapter uses a hyperbolic reversal: death, the ultimate இன்னாதது (painful thing), becomes இனிது (sweet) — the emphatic அதூஉம், ‘even that’ — at the point where giving is no longer possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). The claim measures the worth of a life by its capacity to give: a life without that capacity is, for the generous person, worse than no life. Commentators read it as describing either the giver who has lost his means or one who faces a suppliant with nothing left to offer. The closing hyperbole makes giving not merely a virtue among others but the very thing that makes life worth living, bringing the chapter to a climax.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, King Shibi is tested by gods who take the form of a hawk chasing a dove. When the dove seeks refuge with him, Shibi refuses to give it up and instead offers the hawk an equal weight of his own flesh, finally placing his whole body on the scales rather than fail to give protection.
hinduism.explanation: Shibi would rather give up his life than fail to give what is asked of him.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies the Kural’s claim that for the generous, being unable to give is worse than death.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, story of King Shibi (Sivi)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong narrative illustration of valuing giving above life, framed as protection of a refugee rather than charity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour... Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says death would be gain for him; the only reason to go on living is to serve others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, life’s value is measured by what one can give to others; without that, death is preferable.
christianity._accuracy_note: Loose structural parallel; Paul’s preference for death is about union with Christ, not the inability to give.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allāh] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, ‘My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be of the righteous.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pictures a dying person whose deepest regret is not having given charity while they could.
islam.tie_back: Links death and the lost chance to give, as the Kural does.
islam._accuracy_note: Shared theme of death and the inability to give, but reversed: the Qur’an’s person wants more life to give, the Kural’s giver prefers death to a life without giving.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that righteousness (tzedakah, a word later used for charity) saves from death, while ill-gotten treasure is useless.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties giving and death together, treating righteousness/charity as what gives life its value.
judaism._accuracy_note: Loose parallel; rabbinic tradition reads ‘tzedakah’ here as charity, but the verse does not say death is preferable to being unable to give.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sivi Jataka, King Sivi, who gives alms daily, longs to give something from his own body. When a blind brahmin (Sakka in disguise) asks for an eye, he gladly gives both eyes, and is later rewarded with divine sight.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta king values the chance to give more than his own body and sight.
buddhism.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s attitude that for a true giver, giving outweighs even the greatest personal loss.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; parallel on putting giving above self-preservation, not on preferring death to an inability to give.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Alcestis, when no one else will die in place of King Admetus, his wife Alcestis gives her own life for him, choosing death over a life in which she could not give him the gift of survival.
greek_mythology.explanation: Alcestis treats giving, even of her own life, as more important than living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects the Kural’s scale of values in which giving outweighs life itself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a self-sacrifice myth, only loosely related to the Kural’s claim about being unable to give.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He would prefer a short period of intense pleasure to a long one of mild enjoyment, a twelvemonth of noble life to many years of humdrum existence, and one great and noble action to many trivial ones.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the good person will give up wealth and even life for friends and country, because a short noble life beats a long empty one.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures life by the noble giving it makes possible, not by its length.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good parallel on valuing noble self-giving above mere survival; not specifically about the inability to give charity.
